Canvas and Spore rendering

Canvas owns the window, workspace, focus, input lifecycle and pixels. A Spore owns application state and describes what it wants drawn. It never receives a framebuffer, texture, path, socket or window handle. A Spore is a signed wasm component whose imports are exactly the capabilities its manifest grants; a view is not a Spore and has no authority of its own.

Rust and Lua reach that boundary through the same versioned soil-scene document. The host validates the document against a budget, binds input to an owner generation, and draws it with the renderer it already uses for every other surface. The document is the payload; Canvas remains the only presenter.

What each layer owns

LayerOwnsDoes not own
CanvasWindow and workspace composition, focus, input lifecycle, theme, rasterizer and frame pacingSpore state, application semantics or chart calculations
soil-sceneThe schema-1 scene vocabulary, semantic inks and validation ceilingsDevice handles, host policy or a rasterizer
soil-sdk-canvasThe Rust guest builder and the present callsHost extent, validation or pixels
soil-canvas-hostPer-invocation budget, validation, generation and presenter transportUI behaviour or a second renderer
Lua UI librariesPortable tree, one-pass layout, semantic tokens and document constructionHost measurement, retained state or pixels
soil-runtimeThe legacy core-Wasm present() host used by the S22 reference surfaceA second contract or renderer
Canvas rendererRasterization and composition of the granted surfaceApplication data or layout policy

soil-runtime and soil-canvas-host implement the same WIT contract. Component Spores use soil-canvas-host; the core-Wasm adapter remains for the older S22 surface. New guest work should use the component path.

The rendering path

Rust: soil_sdk::canvas::Surface::present_scene
Lua:  ui.present(tree, theme) or ui.capture(...)
                         |
                         v
              soil-scene document
          { kind: "scene", schema: 1 }
                         |
                         v
       host validation, budget, generation
                         |
                         v
      Canvas presenter -> ui.sock -> renderer

The guest gets one granted surface. soil:canvas is an explicit host-shell capability, not a generic application permission. It may present one document per invocation and deliver one normalized input event. There is no frame callback, no shared scene graph and no guest-owned swapchain. A rejected document keeps the last good frame visible; a stale generation cannot move the owner backwards.

One document, two SDKs

StepRustLua
Build a documentsoil_scene::Scene or soil_scene::Presentui.document(tree, theme) or ui.capture(...)
Present a prepared documentSurface::presentui.present_document(document)
Build and presentSurface::present_sceneui.present(...)
Present pixelsSurface::present_rgbaNot a tree path
Present a GPU leaseSurface::present_leasePlacement not exposed to the tree

The Rust SDK is re-exported as soil_sdk::canvas behind the canvas feature. The Lua libraries emit the same soil-scene document and call the host's canvas.present, or soil.canvas.present on a non-Canvas host. Neither path links a Rust renderer into Lua, and neither path gives the view a device handle.

use soil_sdk::canvas::Surface;
use soil_scene::{Content, Node, Rect, Scene, Transform};

let scene = Scene::new(vec![Node {
    id: "panel".into(),
    parent: None,
    transform: Transform {
        scale: [4.0, 2.0, 1.0],
        ..Transform::default()
    },
    content: Content::Rect(Rect::default()),
    transition_ms: None,
}]);

let state = Surface::present_scene(&scene)?;

local tree = ui.column {
  children = {
    ui.text("Throughput", { style = "title" }),
    ui.stat { label = "Requests", value = 42, unit = "%" },
  },
}

-- Pure artifact: inspect or test it without a compositor.
local document = ui.document(tree, module.theme)

-- Same document, presented through the granted host capability.
ui.present_document(document)

In a Canvas Lua module the library is available as ui. The painter-style fungos.ui adapter exposes the same path through ui.capture(...) and ui.present(width, height, theme, paint).

The wire document

A scene document is JSON with flat nodes. Positions are already resolved by the guest's layout pass; the host does not re-interpret a widget tree.

{
  "kind": "scene",
  "schema": 1,
  "nodes": [
    {
      "id": "panel",
      "transform": {
        "translation": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
        "rotation": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
        "scale": [4.0, 2.0, 1.0]
      },
      "type": "rect",
      "ink": "surface",
      "opacity": 1.0,
      "radius": 8.0
    }
  ]
}
  • kind selects scene, rgba or gpu_lease. scene is the portable path; the other two carry pixels or a lease.
  • schema is 1. A host refuses a version it does not implement.
  • Nodes are flat. A node's parent must name an earlier node in the same document.
  • Canvas presents scene coordinates centred and aspect-free: x and y span -4 to 4, and z controls depth. Scale is in eighths of the surface span, so [4.0, 2.0, 1.0] is half the width and a quarter of the height.
  • Inks are semantic: text, muted, surface, background, primary, success, warning, danger and info. The theme owns their values. An optional literal rgb is for identity colours, not for ordinary UI.
  • The document carries no paths, sockets, textures, raw keycodes or window handles.

The schema ceiling is 4,096 nodes and 32 MiB per payload. A host may enforce a smaller budget: a Canvas Lua module defaults to 1,024 nodes and 256 KiB of source. Rust guests can read Surface::budget() instead of hard-coding a host budget.

Layout, state and controls

There are two layout paths, and they answer different questions.

  • canvas.layout is the native host path. It solves a flex tree through soil-layout (Taffy) with measured text; unibus uses it for its inbox.
  • The portable Lua path in sdk/ui/ui.lua lays out a tree in one pass with no host measurement. The same tree can be previewed and tested without a compositor.

Both paths end at the same scene vocabulary. A view returns a tree; the library places it; the host draws it. A view holds no state and receives no callbacks. ui.action("save") emits an intent, and the Spore decides what it means. State stays in the Spore because Canvas runs a fresh sandbox per render.

Buttons and host surfaces remain host-owned controls. They are hit regions, not scene nodes. widget.hit registers a view's hit targets with the host; the host keeps focus, pointer routing and the button's actual appearance. ui.host_surface reserves layout space and calls canvas.host_resource; it never touches pixels or receives a texture handle.

Dense time series are bounded before they become nodes. ui.lttb keeps the endpoints and the dominant point in each bucket, and ui.chart applies it to series that exceed the chart's mark count. A million-point series stays a host-side GPU resource, not a million-node Lua tree.

Compatibility and rendering coverage

ui.render uses the legacy canvas.rect and canvas.text primitives. It is the compatibility path for a host that predates the scene document. ui.present falls back to it when the host does not grant canvas.present, so an older Canvas keeps drawing instead of going blank. The fallback uses the same layout and tokens; it is not a second renderer.

Canvas refuses a module that mixes canvas.present with canvas.rect or canvas.text in one render. A module chooses a document path or a primitive path, not both.

The Canvas bridge currently draws Rect and Text. The schema accepts Polyline, Area, Band, Points, Heatmap, Candles, Shader, GpuDense and GpuPoints3D, but the bridge maps those nodes to groups so a newer producer's scene survives an older host. This is compatibility, not a chart renderer: a Spore that needs the full vocabulary should use a presenter backed by the native soil-scene-gpu renderer.

GPU surfaces

A Lua tree can reserve a place for a GPU surface; it cannot become one. The native GraphGPU dashboard, the 20k-point cloud and the dense time-series renderer keep their data, decimation and wgpu draw in a native host.

  • A native producer renders into a shared frame buffer and publishes a monotonic revision.
  • Present::GpuLease presents a lease for the granted surface; Canvas owns its extent and composition.
  • ui.host_surface is the Lua placement point. It reserves a rect and calls the host resource API; a renderable GpuLease resource kind is not implemented yet. It does not receive pixels or a GPU handle.

A 1200x840 RGBA frame is about 4 MB, or about 242 MB/s at 60 Hz. Shared memory avoids base64, but it is still a frame copy; a true texture lease is not implemented. The Lua tree cannot reproduce the native 60 Hz path by emitting one node per point, and the compositor should not grow a second chart renderer to pretend otherwise.

Status

CapabilityState

Rust guest SDK and host adapterImplemented
Lua document construction and presentationImplemented
canvas.present in the Canvas module hostImplemented
Legacy primitive fallbackImplemented
Rect and Text through the Canvas bridgeImplemented
Chart and point primitives through the Canvas bridgeAccepted by the schema; rendered as empty groups
GPU lease placement inside a Lua treeNot implemented

The schema is the stable part. Renderer coverage and host-resource placement can improve without changing the document a view produces.

Try it

From a Soil checkout:

cargo test -p soil-scene -p soil-sdk-canvas -p soil-canvas-host
cargo check -p soil-sdk-canvas --target wasm32-wasip2

From a Spores checkout, the Lua document fixture runs without a compositor:

cd spores/gallery
lua tests/soil_fixture.lua

Where it fits

Canvas is a compositor and workspace owner, not an application framework. Soil owns the guest contract and host adapter; Spores own the Lua UI library and component catalog; applications own their state and their decisions. This keeps one renderer, one input lifecycle and one place where pixels live.
